When the data-generating process is known, a simulation study shows how
an estimation procedure behaves: whether its estimates are biased, whether
its standard errors match the actual variability, and whether its
intervals cover the true value as often as they claim. This vignette builds
a small study step by step. Its replicate counts are chosen to keep the
vignette quick; they illustrate the workflow and do not establish the
properties of any method. A parameterized script for a full-size study is
included with the package (see the end).

```{r setup}
library(flexCountReg)
```

## 1. Design the study before generating data

The estimand is the coefficient $\beta_x$ of a covariate $x$ in a
log-linear count model with an exposure offset:

$$E[Y_i] = t_i \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_x x_i), \quad
\beta_0 = 0.5, \; \beta_x = 0.4, \;
x_i \sim N(0, 1), \; t_i \sim U(0.5, 2).$$

The counts are Poisson or NB2 with $\alpha = 0.5$, with $n = 100$ or
$400$ independent rows. Two procedures are compared on every dataset: a
Poisson model and an NB2 model, both with Hessian-based standard errors
and 95% Wald intervals.

```{r scenarios}
scenarios <- expand.grid(family = c("POISSON", "NB2"), n = c(100, 400),
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
scenarios$beta0 <- 0.5
scenarios$beta_x <- 0.4
scenarios$alpha <- ifelse(scenarios$family == "NB2", 0.5, NA)
scenarios$id <- seq_len(nrow(scenarios))
scenarios
```

## 2. A generator that can be checked

The data are generated with base R's `rpois()` and `rnbinom()`, so the
generator is independent of the code being evaluated:

```{r generator}
generate <- function(sc) {
  x <- rnorm(sc$n)
  t <- runif(sc$n, 0.5, 2)
  mu <- t * exp(sc$beta0 + sc$beta_x * x)
  y <- if (sc$family == "POISSON") rpois(sc$n, mu) else
    rnbinom(sc$n, size = 1 / sc$alpha, mu = mu)
  data.frame(y, x, log_t = log(t))
}
```

Two checks against independent results. First, with $\alpha = 1$ the NB2
distribution is geometric, so the generator's frequencies must match
`dgeom()`:

```{r check-geometric}
set.seed(1)
draws <- rnbinom(1e5, size = 1, mu = 2)
round(rbind(simulated = tabulate(draws + 1, 6) / 1e5,
            geometric = dgeom(0:5, prob = 1 / 3)), 4)
```

Second, the package's own `simulate()` method, used later for fitted
models, must reproduce the NB2 mean and variance at the fitted parameters:

```{r check-simulate}
set.seed(2)
d <- generate(scenarios[scenarios$family == "NB2" & scenarios$n == 400, ])
fit <- countreg(y ~ x + offset(log_t), data = d, family = "NB2",
                method = "BFGS")
sims <- simulate(fit, nsim = 2000, seed = 3)
mu <- predict(fit)
alpha <- exp(coef(fit)[["ln(alpha)"]])
summary(data.frame(mean_ratio = rowMeans(sims) / mu,
                   var_ratio = apply(sims, 1, var) / (mu + alpha * mu^2)))
```

Both ratios are centred on 1, with the spread expected from 2,000 draws.

## 3. One replicate, with its status

A replicate generates one dataset, applies each procedure, and returns
one row per procedure. Failures and warnings are recorded, not dropped:

```{r replicate}
fit_one <- function(d, family) {
  warn <- character(0)
  m <- tryCatch(
    withCallingHandlers(
      countreg(y ~ x + offset(log_t), data = d, family = family,
               method = "BFGS"),
      warning = function(w) {
        warn <<- c(warn, conditionMessage(w))
        invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
      }),
    error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(m, "error")) {
    return(data.frame(estimate = NA, se = NA, status = "error",
                      note = conditionMessage(m)))
  }
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  status <- if (!isTRUE(m$model$converged)) "not converged" else
    if (length(warn)) "warning" else "ok"
  data.frame(estimate = co["x", 1], se = co["x", 2], status = status,
             note = paste(warn, collapse = "; "))
}

one_replicate <- function(sc, rep) {
  d <- generate(sc)
  out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("POISSON", "NB2"), function(proc)
    cbind(scenario = sc$id, rep = rep, procedure = proc, fit_one(d, proc))))
  out$truth <- sc$beta_x
  out
}
```

## 4. Reproducible random numbers

Each replicate gets its own stream of the L'Ecuyer-CMRG generator, derived
from one seed. The results do not depend on the order in which replicates
are run, so the same streams can be used by parallel workers (for example
with `parallel::mclapply()` or `future.apply`), and any single replicate can
be rerun on its own:

```{r streams}
RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG")
set.seed(2026)
make_streams <- function(k) {
  s <- .Random.seed
  lapply(seq_len(k), function(i) s <<- parallel::nextRNGStream(s))
}
R <- 100
streams <- make_streams(nrow(scenarios) * R)
run_scenario <- function(sc) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(R), function(r) {
    assign(".Random.seed", streams[[(sc$id - 1) * R + r]],
           envir = globalenv())
    one_replicate(sc, r)
  }))
}
results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(scenarios, scenarios$id),
                                 run_scenario))
results <- merge(scenarios[c("id", "family", "n")], results,
                 by.x = "id", by.y = "scenario")
head(results)
table(results$procedure, results$status)
```

The result is a tidy table with one row per scenario, replicate and
procedure. Notes on warnings are kept with the row they belong to.

## 5. Summaries with Monte Carlo standard errors

For each scenario and procedure: bias, empirical standard deviation of the
estimates, mean reported standard error, root mean squared error and the
coverage of the 95% Wald interval, each with its Monte Carlo standard error
(MCSE). Summaries use the successful fits; the attempted and successful
counts are shown so that the conditioning is visible.

```{r summarize}
summarize_sim <- function(res) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(split(res, list(res$id, res$procedure)),
                        function(d) {
    ok <- d$status %in% c("ok", "warning") & is.finite(d$se)
    e <- d$estimate[ok]
    se <- d$se[ok]
    k <- sum(ok)
    cover <- abs(e - d$truth[ok]) <= qnorm(0.975) * se
    data.frame(data = d$family[1], n = d$n[1], procedure = d$procedure[1],
               attempted = nrow(d), used = k,
               bias = mean(e - d$truth[ok]), mcse_bias = sd(e) / sqrt(k),
               emp_sd = sd(e), mean_se = mean(se),
               rmse = sqrt(mean((e - d$truth[ok])^2)),
               coverage = mean(cover),
               mcse_coverage = sqrt(mean(cover) * (1 - mean(cover)) / k))
  }))
}
summary_table <- summarize_sim(results)
summary_table[order(summary_table$data, summary_table$n), -c(4, 5)] |>
  format(digits = 3)
summary_table[, c("data", "n", "procedure", "attempted", "used")]
```

```{r summary-text, include = FALSE}
st <- summary_table
pois_on_nb <- st[st$data == "NB2" & st$procedure == "POISSON", ]
nb_on_nb <- st[st$data == "NB2" & st$procedure == "NB2", ]
n_warn <- sum(results$status == "warning")
```

On NB2 data, the Poisson procedure's reported standard errors are much
smaller than the actual spread of its estimates (for $n = 400$, a mean
standard error of `r round(pois_on_nb$mean_se[pois_on_nb$n == 400], 3)`
against an empirical standard deviation of
`r round(pois_on_nb$emp_sd[pois_on_nb$n == 400], 3)`), so its intervals
cover the true value only
`r round(100 * pois_on_nb$coverage[pois_on_nb$n == 400])`% of the time
(MCSE `r round(100 * pois_on_nb$mcse_coverage[pois_on_nb$n == 400], 1)`
points). The NB2 procedure's coverage is
`r round(100 * nb_on_nb$coverage[nb_on_nb$n == 400])`%. Both
estimators are nearly unbiased: the Poisson estimator is consistent for
$\beta_x$ under NB2 data, but its standard errors are not.

With `r R` replicates, a coverage estimate near 95% has an MCSE of about
2.2 percentage points, too large to distinguish 93% from 95%. Differences
smaller than about two MCSEs are not evidence of anything.

`r n_warn` of the `r nrow(results)` fits gave a warning. These are NB2 fits to
Poisson data, where the dispersion approaches its boundary (see
`vignette("numerical-reliability", package = "flexCountReg")`). They are
kept in the summaries, because the coefficient of $x$ is still estimated
well; a study whose target was the dispersion would have to treat them
separately.

## 6. Panel data: keep the independent unit

With repeated measurements, the independent unit is the group, and the
generator must give all rows of a group one shared effect. Here, 100 units
are each observed 5 times, with a gamma-distributed unit effect (mean 1,
variance 0.5), a unit-level covariate $z$ and a row-level covariate $x$:

```{r panel-generator}
generate_panel <- function(n_units = 100, T = 5, theta = 0.5) {
  id <- rep(seq_len(n_units), each = T)
  u <- rgamma(n_units, shape = 1 / theta, rate = 1 / theta)[id]
  z <- rnorm(n_units)[id]
  x <- rnorm(n_units * T)
  data.frame(id, z, x, y = rpois(n_units * T, u * exp(0.2 + 0.4 * z +
                                                        0.3 * x)))
}
```

The negative multinomial model of `negmultinom()` (family `"NM2"`, the
default) matches this process: Poisson counts given a gamma unit effect
with mean 1 and variance $\alpha$ (here 0.5), shared by the rows of a unit.
The pooled Poisson model ignores the grouping:

```{r panel-study}
panel_rep <- function(r) {
  assign(".Random.seed", panel_streams[[r]], envir = globalenv())
  d <- generate_panel()
  est <- function(m, nm) {
    co <- summary(m)$coefficients
    c(estimate = co[nm, 1], se = co[nm, 2])
  }
  pooled <- countreg(y ~ z + x, data = d, family = "POISSON",
                     method = "BFGS")
  nm <- negmultinom(y ~ z + x, group_var = "id", data = d)
  rbind(data.frame(rep = r, procedure = "pooled Poisson",
                   term = c("z", "x"),
                   rbind(est(pooled, "z"), est(pooled, "x")),
                   converged = pooled$model$converged),
        data.frame(rep = r, procedure = "negative multinomial",
                   term = c("z", "x"), rbind(est(nm, "z"), est(nm, "x")),
                   converged = nm$model$converged))
}
R_panel <- 100
panel_streams <- make_streams(R_panel)
panel <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(R_panel), panel_rep))
panel$truth <- ifelse(panel$term == "z", 0.4, 0.3)
panel$cover <- abs(panel$estimate - panel$truth) <=
  qnorm(0.975) * panel$se
aggregate(cbind(estimate, se, cover, converged) ~ procedure + term,
          data = panel, FUN = mean)
aggregate(estimate ~ procedure + term, data = panel, FUN = sd)
```

The pooled model's standard error for the unit-level covariate $z$ is far
below the spread of its estimates, and its intervals undercover; the
negative multinomial model accounts for the shared effect. Bootstrap or
cross-validation in such a study must also resample whole units, never
rows (`stderr = "boot"` in the panel models does this).

## 7. A full-size study

The package includes a parameterized script for a larger version of this
study:

```{r script-path}
script <- system.file("validation", "simulation-studies",
                      "count-regression-study.R", package = "flexCountReg")
file.exists(script)
```

(`script` holds its location on your computer.) It runs the scenarios
above with a chosen number of replicates (the
environment variable `REPS`, default 1000) and seed (`SEED`), using one
random-number stream per replicate, and writes the replicate results, the
summary table, and a record of the settings, R and package versions and
the random-number generator. Run it from a terminal, for example:

```
REPS=1000 SEED=2026 Rscript count-regression-study.R
```

A companion script, `inst/validation/finite-mixtures/mixture-recovery-study.R`,
applies the same design to finite-mixture and latent-class models
(`vignette("latent-class-regression", package = "flexCountReg")`). Two
features are specific to mixtures. First, component labels are arbitrary,
so component-specific estimands are compared after a documented
alignment (there, the display order of the components), and a
label-invariant estimand (the mixture mean at a reference point) is
reported alongside them. Second, panel scenarios generate one class per
panel, so whole panels must be generated and resampled. The script also
records how many starts reached each selected solution.

## Checklist

* Write down the estimand, the scenarios and the procedures first.
* Check the generator against independent special cases.
* Return a status for every fit; never drop failures silently.
* Report MCSEs and the number of attempted and used replicates.
* Use independent, reproducible random-number streams per replicate.
* In panel designs, generate and resample whole units.
* Record the seed, settings and software versions with the results.

```{r restore-rng, include = FALSE}
do.call(RNGkind, as.list(old_rng))
```
